subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: choosing one course and finishing it [Action]
passage: Neel had six browser tabs of coding courses open, each promising to make him a programmer in thirty days. On Sunday he closed five, bookmarked one beginner Python course and stuck a note above his desk: One lesson a day. No new course until this one ends. His sister Nikita teased him when he refused to open a trending video about a shiny new language. Neel typed every example himself, then changed a number to see what would happen. Twenty-eight days later he finished the last lesson and wrote a tiny program of his own that counted the days to Nikita's birthday and printed a message. It was off by one on the first run. He fixed it without help and grinned at the screen.

qa.q: What did Neel write on the note above his desk?
qa.a: One lesson a day, and no new course until this one ends.

qa.q: How might Neel have felt when he refused the trending video?
qa.a: Tempted but determined: he held to his rule even though a new course looked exciting.

qa.q: What else could Neel do to make his practice stick, and why?
qa.a: Change each example and predict the result before running it, since testing his own guesses builds skill beyond copying.

qa.q: How does Neel's plan look to Nikita?
qa.a: Nikita sees her brother ignore the trend and stick with one course; she teases him, but may be impressed when he finishes and builds something for her.

grounding: A student picks one beginner course, sets one lesson a day, resists other courses and writes a small program of his own.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: learning by building a tiny project [Action]
passage: Gargi had forty minutes a night after homework, and a laptop she shared with her father. She decided to build a quiz for her class's history test. She typed ten questions into a Python list. She learned what a for-loop was because she needed to go through the questions, and learned input() because she needed the answers. When the score wouldn't add up, she searched the error, found she had typed the number as text, and fixed it. On Friday her classmate Suraj tried the quiz, scored seven out of ten and asked, “Can you make one for geography?” By the next week a dozen classmates had copied the file to the school lab computers. It was untidy, and it worked.

qa.q: How many minutes did Gargi have each night?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How might Gargi have felt when the score would not add up?
qa.a: Frustrated and stuck at first, but she searched the error instead of giving up 🙂.

qa.q: What else could Gargi do to improve the quiz, and why?
qa.a: Ask classmates which questions confused them and add more, since real use shows what is needed.

qa.q: How does the quiz look to Suraj?
qa.a: Suraj gets a lively way to revise and asks for geography, so it feels useful instead of like another assignment.

grounding: A teen builds a quiz for classmates, learning only the loops, lists and input she needs, and ends with something friends use.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
passage: For three months I watched coding videos every night. Loops, functions, lists: I nodded along and felt like I was getting somewhere. Then my cousin Sarika, who builds websites for a living, handed me her laptop with a blank editor and said, “Print the numbers 1 to 10.” I sat there for twenty minutes. When the tutor typed a loop it looked obvious. Alone, I couldn't type one. My face went hot and I felt stupid. Sarika didn't laugh. She said, “Watching isn't typing.” I realised I had not written a single line of my own in ninety days. I had only been following someone else's hands. — Deepak

qa.q: What did Sarika ask Deepak to do in the blank editor?
qa.a: Print the numbers 1 to 10.

qa.q: What did Deepak feel while staring at the blank editor?
qa.a: Embarrassed and shaken: Deepak felt hot and stupid because knowing a loop by watching was not the same as writing one.

qa.q: What could Deepak do instead, and why?
qa.a: Type each example, then close the video and rewrite it from memory, since writing it alone builds real recall.

qa.q: How does Deepak's habit look to Sarika?
qa.a: Sarika, who builds websites, has likely seen this before and does not laugh, but wants Deepak to see that watching is different from typing.

grounding: A student watches tutorial after tutorial, feels sure of learning, but cannot write a loop in a blank editor.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: debugging by reading the error and isolating the cause [Thinking]
passage:
“It crashed again.” Reena leaned in close. “Devika, don't tell me. Let me read it.”
“Go on.”
“IndexError, list index out of range, line fourteen.” Reena frowned. “Line fourteen. Not line one, so the whole program isn't wrong.”
“Where's the list?”
“Line nine. Five items.” Reena counted under the breath. “And the loop goes up to six. Off by one?”
“Maybe. How could you check?”
“Comment out the bottom half first. If it runs, the trouble is down there.” Reena typed hash marks. The program ran. “Okay, bottom half.” Reena changed the six to a five and ran it. “One change. Works.”
Devika smiled. “Only one?”
“One at a time, or I'll never know which fixed it.”

qa.q: Which line did the error message point to?
qa.a: Line fourteen.

qa.q: What might Reena be feeling when asking Devika not to tell the answer?
qa.a: Determined and a little proud: Reena wants to work it out alone 🙂.

qa.q: What could Reena do if the error came back after the fix, and why?
qa.a: Print the values inside the loop and change one thing at a time, since checking after every change shows which change matters.

qa.q: How does Reena's approach look to Devika?
qa.a: Devika, who only asks questions, sees Reena reasoning step by step, and may feel it is better to let Reena find the fix than to hand it over.

grounding: A teen faced with a crash reads the error, isolates the cause by commenting out half the code and fixes one thing at a time.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: copying and pasting code without understanding [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Afreen, and I share the lab computer with Faisal. His Python homework was a program to average marks, and it ran perfectly. He had pasted it from a forum. Then the teacher said, “Add a line to ignore any zero mark.” Faisal stared at the screen for a long time. He tried another forum snippet; the program crashed. He scrolled up and down and muttered, “I don't know what line six does.” I can't be sure how he felt, but his ears went red. He stayed after school to redo it and missed his bus. I noticed that the code had looked so clever at first, and fell apart the moment anyone touched it.

qa.q: What was Faisal's homework program supposed to do?
qa.a: Average marks.

qa.q: How did Faisal probably feel when the teacher asked for a small change?
qa.a: Embarrassed and stuck: he stared at the screen and his ears went red, though Afreen cannot be certain of his feelings.

qa.q: What could Faisal do instead of pasting, and why?
qa.a: Read each pasted line, write what it does in his own words and change one thing at a time, since knowing why a line is there lets him modify it.

qa.q: How does the pasted program look to Afreen?
qa.a: Afreen sees it work at first and then fail at the smallest change, so it seems clever but hollow.

grounding: A student pastes forum answers until the program runs, then cannot modify it because he never understood the lines.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: setting a schedule around slow internet and shared device [Thinking]
passage: Nour's family had one phone with a small data plan and one laptop that Nour's mother needed until six. So Nour made a schedule instead of complaining. Every Tuesday and Saturday after school, Nour went to the library, sat by the window where the wifi was strongest, and downloaded the next four lessons plus the exercise files. From seven to eight-thirty each evening the laptop was Nour's, offline, working through those exercises. On the bus, Nour reread notes on the phone without using any data. Tuan, from the same class, asked how it was done. “I stopped waiting for the perfect setup,” Nour said, “and planned around the one I have.” The plan wasn't fast, but it never stalled.

qa.q: When could Nour use the laptop?
qa.a: From seven to eight-thirty each evening.

qa.q: What might Nour feel about the limits, judging from the choices made?
qa.a: Practical and determined, perhaps a little frustrated, but choosing to plan around the limits instead of complaining.

qa.q: What else could Nour do to make the offline time count, and why?
qa.a: Write the exercise steps in a notebook while at the library so they can be tried offline, since it uses the limited hours well.

qa.q: How might Nour's mother see the plan?
qa.a: Nour's mother, who needs the laptop until six, sees a child working around her schedule instead of demanding time, which feels fair.

grounding: A teen with a family phone and patchy data plans downloads at the library and codes offline in a fixed slot on a shared laptop.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: joining a study group for accountability [Action]
passage: Coding club teacher's note, Friday. Samir has been meeting two classmates in the library every Friday at 4:15. The rule: each person solves one problem during the week and presents the solution to the other two. Week three was a dull one, with exams and heat, and I saw Samir skip. The others didn't scold. One sent a message: “We start at 4:15, need your loop.” Samir turned up with half a solution, and the three finished it together. Nobody has missed since. All I did was give them a corner and a whiteboard. Samir told me, “If it were only me, I'd have quit in week three.” — Zainab

qa.q: When does the study group meet?
qa.a: Every Friday at 4:15.

qa.q: What might Samir be feeling when admitting to quitting in week three without the group?
qa.a: Grateful and a bit relieved: the group's nudge kept Samir going through a dull week.

qa.q: What else could the group do to keep going, and why?
qa.a: Take turns choosing the weekly problem, since shared ownership keeps everyone invested.

qa.q: How does the group look to the classmate who sent the message?
qa.a: That classmate probably feels responsible for the group and glad Samir came, and the kind nudge kept it friendly instead of scolding.

grounding: A student teams with two classmates to solve and present one problem a week and nudge whoever skips.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: perfectionism stalls the first version [Pitfall]
passage: For four weeks Gopika had been building a timetable planner in Python, and she had nothing that ran. Every time she looked at her code she saw mess: a function called do_stuff, files named badly. So she deleted it and started again. She renamed folders planner_final, planner_final2, planner_new. She read three style guides and picked a colour theme for her editor. The school coding fair was in nine days. Farhan, beside her, said, “Just get one button working.” “It'll look bad.” On the morning of the fair Gopika had a folder of tidy, empty files, and on the next table sat Farhan's rough, slightly ugly calculator, working.

qa.q: How many weeks had Gopika been building the planner?
qa.a: Four weeks.

qa.q: What might Gopika be feeling when she says it will look bad?
qa.a: Embarrassed and afraid of judgment: fear of messy code keeps her from finishing anything.

qa.q: What could Gopika do instead, and why?
qa.a: Build a rough working version first and tidy it afterwards, since something that runs can be improved while empty files cannot.

qa.q: How does Gopika's habit look to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan sees someone capable stuck restarting when a rough version could already run, so Farhan urges Gopika to get one button working.

grounding: A teen keeps restarting because the structure feels messy, spends a month on setup and never reaches a working first version.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: reviewing progress and changing method [Revision]
passage: “Sumit, you know me, Chaitanya, the boy with the big plans. So here's what happened. Three weeks in, I noticed I hadn't learned anything new. I opened my log to see what I'd been doing: video, video, video. I could nod along with anyone, but if you asked me to write a loop I couldn't. That was embarrassing, honestly. So I flipped it. Now I try a small exercise first, like printing a pattern of stars, and I only open a video when I'm truly stuck. The first week I hated it. By week five I had written a number-guessing game with my own hands. It was a small game, but it was mine, and I could explain every line.”

qa.q: What did Chaitanya see when he opened his log?
qa.a: Video, video, video: he had only been watching.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya feel about the three weeks with nothing new?
qa.a: Embarrassed and disappointed, since he could nod along but could not write a loop himself.

qa.q: What else could Chaitanya do to check his progress, and why?
qa.a: Ask a friend to look at his exercises each week, since outside feedback can catch gaps he cannot see.

qa.q: How does the change look to Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit, hearing this from Chaitanya, sees someone who noticed a lack of progress and changed method, and may feel encouraged to check personal habits too.

grounding: After three weeks without new skills, a student reviews his log, sees he only watched, and switches to exercises first.

subtopic: Learning to code from the internet
subtype: Approach: asking for help with a well-formed question [Action]
passage: “Pallavi, thanks for having me. I'm Afreen, and I was stuck on one bug for two days: my program printed 0 for the total. At first I posted in a learner forum, ‘It doesn't work, please help,’ and got nothing. Silence. So I tried again and wrote three things: I expected 45, I got 0, and here's what I already tried, printing every value and renaming the variable, plus the ten lines. Within a day a stranger replied that I'd set total to zero inside the loop, so it reset every time. I moved that line above the loop, and there was my 45. It felt like magic, but really it was just a clearer question.”

qa.q: What did Afreen expect the program to print?
qa.a: A total of 45.

qa.q: How did Afreen feel after the first post got no reply?
qa.a: Discouraged and ignored: the vague message brought only silence.

qa.q: What else could Afreen do if no one replied, and why?
qa.a: Ask a teacher or classmate to read the ten lines, since a person nearby can often spot a mistake quickly.

qa.q: How does the well-formed question look to the stranger who answered?
qa.a: The stranger can see the expected result, the actual result and what was tried, so a quick answer is possible, whereas a vague post would need many follow-up questions.

grounding: A teen stuck on a bug writes what was expected, what happened and what was tried, and gets a useful answer within a day.
